title: The green twig bends
hookLine: living things are soft and supple, dead things hard and stiff (Tao Te Ching 76)
carry: the soft and yielding are companions of life

cards: Try to snap a green twig on a bush, and it won't break cleanly. It bends, folds over, and hangs on by a strip of bark. Now try a dead stick from the ground: one quick crack, and it's two pieces.

Same plant, maybe, same thickness. The difference is that one is alive. Chapter seventy-six of the Tao Te Ching builds a whole teaching on that crack, starting not with plants but with the human body.

teach.b: First, the body. When people are born, the chapter says, they're soft and supple; when they die, they're hard and stiff. That's not a metaphor yet.
It's just what a body does.
Grass and trees, alive, are soft and tender; dead, they're dry and brittle. The two pictures sit side by side so the pattern is hard to miss. Third, the conclusion.
So the hard and the stiff are companions of death, it says, and the soft and the yielding are companions of life.
Then the pattern moves into the world of power: an army that's too rigid doesn't win, and a tree that's too stiff meets the axe. The big and hard end up below; the soft and supple end up above.
That reverses what force usually expects.

Fourth, can it still bend? Stiffness shows up in more than joints: a position held so hard there's no room to hear anything, a routine that can't bend for a sick kid, a jaw clenched through a whole meeting.
If something can't bend, it may be less alive than it looks. Soft, here, doesn't mean giving up. The green twig still holds.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter seventy-six as a teaching on flexibility: what is alive bends, what is dead is stiff, and rigid strength tends to break.

games.q: two trees in a storm: one stiff and mighty, one supple. which does chapter seventy-six say meets the axe?
games.why: a tree that's too stiff meets the axe. the big and hard end up below; the soft and supple end up above.

practice: Seated or standing, let the breath lead: on an in-breath, lift the arms or roll the shoulders slowly, and on the out-breath, let them soften.
Find one place that's holding stiff, maybe the jaw, the hands, the lower back, and breathe toward it until it gives a little. Stay within what feels easy; nothing here is a contest.

wordCard.voice: Soft is alive. Chapter seventy-six: living things are soft and supple, dead things hard and stiff; the soft are companions of life. Today's word.
